title: Small-landlord compliance + LTB ops
wedge: A landlord operating system for notices, payment history, maintenance records, deadlines and evidence, designed for one-to-five-unit owners.
buyer: Small Toronto landlord who is not a professional property manager.
painMoment: “I have one bad tenancy and suddenly I need to understand forms, deadlines, evidence and months of cash-flow exposure.”
currentWorkaround: Spreadsheets, property managers, paralegals, ad-hoc templates and forum advice.
whyNow: LTB applications remain at record volumes; non-payment applications make up more than half of cases and are still measured in weeks to first hearing.
firstPaidTest: Enroll 10 landlords and run their records/notices through a structured workflow with a paralegal reviewing legal content.
fitNote: Good workflow/product fit, moderate distribution fit. A strong wedge would be Ontario-specific evidence readiness rather than generic property management.

title: IVF cost + waitlist navigator
wedge: Compare clinic waitlists, funded/private pathways, base fees, medication/add-on costs and dates in one decision timeline.
buyer: Ontario/Toronto patient trying to start IVF on a time-sensitive schedule.
painMoment: “I cannot tell which clinic can actually treat me when I need it, what is funded, or what the real all-in cycle cost will be.”
currentWorkaround: Clinic calls, Reddit, spreadsheets, fertility doctor referrals, separate fee pages.
whyNow: Toronto base IVF fees are commonly five figures and current 2026 patients actively compare funded wait times between downtown clinics.
firstPaidTest: Manually build ten treatment-path comparisons using public fees and current clinic wait-time calls; charge for navigation, not medical recommendations.
riskNotes: Cannot recommend treatment or interpret medical necessity without clinicians.
fitNote: Excellent information-design problem but weak health-domain credibility. Keep to logistics, cost and availability unless clinically partnered.

title: Dental coverage + clinic navigator
wedge: Given income, age, insurance and treatment need, show which public/low-cost programs are available and the shortest realistic care path.
buyer: Toronto resident delaying dental care because coverage and pricing are confusing.
painMoment: “I know I need treatment, but I do not know what is covered, where I qualify, or how much I will pay.”
currentWorkaround: Call 311/public health, search separate federal/provincial programs, dental-school clinics and individual offices.
whyNow: Toronto now points residents across multiple overlapping programs, with separate eligibility rules and a list of low-cost facilities.
firstPaidTest: Build a questionnaire that produces a verified care-path checklist and test it with community organizations before charging consumers.
priceHypothesis: Likely B2B2C / benefits model; C$0–49 consumer
riskNotes: Low direct willingness to pay among people most in need.
fitNote: Strong eligibility/workflow UX fit with low clinical-advice exposure. Better business model may be employers, nonprofits or clinics rather than charging patients.

title: Accessibility retrofit navigator
wedge: Turn mobility needs and a home layout into a staged retrofit plan, grant/tax-credit map, contractor scope and quote comparison.
buyer: Senior, disabled resident or adult child modifying a Toronto home for mobility.
painMoment: “We need this home to be safe before the next fall, but I do not know what to change first or what help pays for it.”
currentWorkaround: Occupational therapist, contractor, tax-credit research, family improvisation.
whyNow: Toronto and federal/provincial programs provide multiple credits/supports while accessibility renovations can range from small modifications to major five-figure projects.
firstPaidTest: Partner with an OT or accessibility contractor and sell a staged home-modification plan before any construction quote is accepted.
fitNote: Good service-design and prioritization fit, but safety/domain expertise must come from qualified accessibility professionals.

title: Primary-care + referral navigator
wedge: Help unattached patients understand Health Care Connect, local team eligibility, walk-in continuity and referral records while waiting for attachment.
buyer: Toronto/Ontario resident without a regular primary-care provider.
painMoment: “I technically have access to health care, but I do not have one person who owns the thread.”
currentWorkaround: Health Care Connect, walk-ins, virtual care, repeated histories, hospital/clinic referrals.
whyNow: Ontario reported roughly 1.98M people unattached to primary care as of September 2025 while rapidly expanding attachment programs in 2026.
firstPaidTest: Test a non-clinical navigation/record-prep service with 20 unattached patients and primary-care clinics.
priceHypothesis: Low direct consumer fee; employer/clinic/insurer model
riskNotes: Cannot guarantee attachment or give medical advice.
Public system changes may reduce the pain over time.
fitNote: Strong workflow and records fit, but business-model and health-domain credibility are weak. Better as infrastructure for providers/employers than direct-to-consumer.
